1.0.0.en: St. Paul the Apostle always boasts and identifies himself as a servant, by his own will, of the Lord Christ, because He loved him first, called him, and chose him as an apostle by appearing to him Himself, and his mission is to preach the good news of the Gospel.

1.0.1.en: The apostleship of St. Paul opens a door of hope for us. As Christ chose him, He wishes to choose you also, beloved brother, in spite of your weak abilities and whatever your past life has been, to be His ambassador among your brethren by your conduct and your upright speech.

1.1.0.en: The Lord Christ is the center of the preaching, and He is the promise for which mankind longed greatly. How often the prophets spoke of Him as a man (the son of David), like us, sharing with us our suffering nature.

1.2.0.en: The Spirit of holiness: The Holy Spirit, by the resurrection of Christ from the dead, revealed to us with power and clarity that He is also the living God who rose from the dead by Himself, by the power of His divinity. We believed in Him by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, whom we received as the greatest gift through the sacrament of the Holy Myron after Baptism. For no one can say that Christ is Lord but by the Holy Spirit.

1.2.1.en: Therefore, my beloved brother, the soul rejoices in Him, for it finds in Him all its needs. He is Jesus the man, who feels with you and suffered as you do; He is Christ the Redeemer, who bore in your place the penalty of suffering and death; and He is the Lord God who rose from the dead, saying to you, beloved: "I have conquered the strongest enemy of mankind, which is death, so why are you afraid? Trust Me, for I am able to solve all your problems."

1.3.0.en: The Lord Christ offered the grace of redemption to all mankind, not because of any merit in us, but because of His love for us, since His delight is with the sons of Adam. He set the apostles apart to proclaim to all the Gentiles that they should accept the truths of the faith with obedience and complete submission from the heart.

1.4.0.en: The Apostle Paul began by directing and addressing his words to the believers in Rome, calling them beloved of God, and saying that Christ calls them to a life of holiness, granting them peace and joy.

1.4.1.en: God calls you to a life of holiness if you obey His commandments, and your life is then filled with peace, that great grace of which the world today is deprived because of its evil. Indeed, the children of the world complain every day of depression and sleeplessness, for "There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22).

1.5.0.en: It is remarkable in this verse that St. Paul rejoices in the faith of the Christians of Rome and thanks God for it, despite the lack of precision and depth in this faith, as we shall see later. But St. Paul teaches us to look for the virtues of others, and to thank God and praise them for these.

1.6.0.en: Here St. Paul draws our attention to the only worship acceptable before God, which is worship in the Spirit (Jn 4:23, 24). In it the believer walks according to the commandments of the Gospel, doing everything through Christ and for His sake, keeping in his heart that God sees all his deeds and the thoughts of his heart, even those that people do not see. Therefore the spiritual person always tries, as far as his strength allows, to please God's heart with love. This is the opposite of formal worship, in which a person is concerned with religiosity before people only, to obtain their praise, while his heart is empty of any love or fear of God.

1.6.1.en: And because St. Paul knew that the delight of God's heart is for sinners to return to the Father's embrace, his heart was kindled with a fatherly love, in imitation of his Christ as a shepherd who seeks His sheep. So Paul remembers the Christians of Rome at all times and prays for them, hoping to visit Rome to preach there and to strengthen the believers in it.

1.7.0.en: St. Paul declares his longing to come to them and see them, not to take anything for himself, but to give them a spiritual gift to strengthen them, in the form of preaching or guidance suited to each one.

1.8.0.en: Here Paul concludes this section by saying that he will rejoice in their faith and they will rejoice in his faith. That is, the servant is encouraged by seeing faith in his children, just as those he serves are strengthened when they see the strength of their servant's faith.

1.8.1.en: Be careful to pray for those around you and those you know, near and far, confident that your prayer opens their hearts to the knowledge of God and strengthens them in it, in addition to deepening your own personal relationship with God first.

1.9.s.en: (3) Paul's longing to preach in Rome

1.9.0.en: Here St. Paul affirms once more the extent of his longing for them, declaring that all the abilities and gifts he has he is ready to offer in his ministry and preaching among them, so that he may rejoice in the fruits of their faith and virtues, explaining that he is a debtor to God, who loved him and died for him. So he offers his love to God's children, mankind, whether Greeks or others (barbarians), and to the learned and the unlearned.

1.9.1.en: And you, beloved, if someone asks you for some service, do not look upon it as toil or effort, but rejoice, for every labor of love offered to God lays up for you a treasure in heaven.

1.10.0.en: Paul boasts that he preaches the Gospel of Christ and is not ashamed of His sufferings and crucifixion, because the Gospel has a power that works in souls. He began preaching to the Jews first, because they are Jews like him and know God and the prophets.

1.11.0.en: The righteousness of God: His justice and His mercy.

1.11.1.en: From faith to faith: Its origin is "from faith to faith." That is, the redemption of Christ transferred us from the first faith in the Old Testament, in which a person, in order to become righteous, had to do the works and commandments of the Law and offer many sacrifices, which were a symbol of Christ, to atone for his sins; to the second faith in the New Testament, which is built on trust in the infinite sacrifice of Christ the Redeemer on the Cross, which atones for the sins of mankind and so justifies those who believe in it.

1.11.2.en: The Gospel revealed to us the righteousness of God, which made us righteous before Him. When Christ died for us, He satisfied divine justice so that we might receive God's mercy and forgiveness. Not every person enjoys this justification, but only the one who lives by faith (Hab 2:4), that is, the one who believes and also obeys His commandments.

1.12.0.en: After Paul encouraged the believers in Rome and praised their faith, he declares God's wrath on the Gentiles who despise God and persist in their sins, and he rejects the sins by which the wicked suppress the truth and conceal it.

1.13.0.en: There is no excuse for a person who claims not to know God, because His voice is within him, and it is the conscience.

1.14.0.en: His invisible things: His divine power hidden behind His works.

1.14.1.en: The things that are made: the creatures.

1.14.2.en: Eternal: everlasting, without beginning or end.

1.14.3.en: For God's living creation, of man, animal, and plant, as well as the inanimate, such as the mountains, seas, planets, and stars, and the wonderful geometric order of nature, declares clearly that there must be a mighty and great God behind this amazing creation. So why do the pagans not believe? They have no excuse for their unbelief.

1.15.0.en: In their ignorance and stupidity, after they knew God, instead of thanking Him for His gifts, people attributed the credit for creation, the universe, and His gifts to idols made in the form of human beings, animals, or birds, and worshiped them.

1.15.1.en: Examine your heart: is it attached to God or to other idols such as money, position, or various desires? Do not remove God from your heart to put anyone or anything in His place, and review yourself at the end of every day: to what extent have you lived with God, and how much have you been occupied with worldly matters?

1.16.s.en: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

1.16.0.en: When man replaced God with idols, which are false, unreal gods, God gave him up to uncleanness. That is, God left the wicked to do evil by their own will, in fornication and perversion by which they dishonored their pure bodies, and they forgot that they were created in the image and likeness of God, after their continual rejection of the work of God's grace. God allowed them to humble themselves, so that perhaps they might repent of their evil and return again to their purity.

1.17.0.en: Because the wicked abandoned God, their vile passions humbled them, such as women turning away from the natural, holy sexual relations that God created, to perverse relations, whether a woman with a woman like herself, or sinful sexual practices with men, but not in the natural organs meant for procreation. Because of the hideousness of this sin, it is counted among the causes of divorce which the Church permits.

1.18.0.en: The men were not content with the sin of fornication, but went beyond it to sexual perversion with one another, that abominable sin which greatly angered God against the people of Sodom, so that He burned it with fire long ago.

1.19.0.en: God forbid that it be God who gave them up to evil with His own hands; rather, they fell by their own will, like a sick man who refused to listen to his doctor's advice, and so his condition worsened. And as a result of their sins they receive punishment, such as fornicators being afflicted with diseases like syphilis, AIDS, and cervical cancer.

1.19.1.en: But why does the merciful God allow this?

1.19.2.en: So that man may realize the effects and torment of sin and its deceit, that perhaps he may repent of it.

1.20.0.en: Because of man's foolishness and stubbornness, instead of repenting of sin, he takes even more pleasure in it, forgetting its pains and its punishment. For this reason St. Paul mentioned this enormous number of sins, to show that a person usually begins with one sin, and that sin drags the rest of the sins after it, so that he is filled with all unrighteousness. The word unrighteousness means all sins in general.

1.21.0.en: Whisperers: those who speak evil of people in secret.

1.21.1.en: Backbiters: those who speak evil and lies openly.

1.21.2.en: Slanderers: those who fall into judging others.

1.21.3.en: Boasters: that is, those who exaggerate in their words and attribute to themselves what they do not have.

1.21.4.en: Inventors of evil things: those who devise new kinds of evil.

1.21.5.en: Disobedient to parents: they refuse to learn, to be disciples, and to benefit from previous experience.

1.22.0.en: Covenantbreakers: that is, one who does not keep his promises to others and does not carry them out. In sum, they are hard-hearted and ignorant.

1.23.0.en: After the wicked knew God's wrath and His punishment of destruction for them, they did not repent but defied Him by encouraging others to sin, as happens now when the media present stimulating films, and young people encourage one another to smoke cigarettes and use drugs, and incite one another to sinful romantic relationships, and encourage sexual freedom as proof of their manhood or womanhood.

1.23.1.en: Therefore, beloved, beware of sin at all its levels, and beware of following the ideas of the world and its freedom, for the whole world lieth in wickedness. And if sin gains mastery over you, pray with faith to your God, who is able to free you from sins, and continue your spiritual striving against it.

1.23.2.en: Thus St. Paul concluded the chapter with a problem in need of a solution, the problem of the sinner sitting in the shadow of death who deserved God's wrath, and who is now in the utmost need of justification in Christ, through faith and by abandoning the works of darkness.

2.0.0.en: St. Paul begins by directing his words to every person who thinks that his knowledge and understanding of God's law place him in a higher rank than other people, so that he judges them and pronounces others guilty as though he were a judge over their faults, while he finds dozens of excuses for himself when he falls into the same faults. He also warns us that the one who judges does those same things, that is, whoever judges another will certainly fall into the same sin one day because he has not been humble. Therefore the verse came plainly: "thou art inexcusable," and you will be subject to judgment, you who judge another.

2.1.0.en: Here St. Paul reminds us of a fact we all know, which is that God's judgment is according to truth. That is, He judges not only by outward appearance but also examines the heart, knowing each person's motives for sin, taking into account the circumstances and environment in which the sinner grew up, aware of each person's measure of spiritual knowledge and whether he committed the sin willingly and intentionally or as a result of weakness. Thus the measure of God's punishment for the same sin differs from one person to another.

2.2.0.en: Here St. Paul mentions a wrong behavior that psychologists know as "projection," in which the sinful person numbs his guilty conscience by talking a great deal about the faults of others.

2.2.1.en: Therefore, beloved, do not think that you are without sin so that you judge others. Do you know that not paying the tithes is the sin of theft, or that whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart, and that abortion is murder? Indeed, gossip itself is counted as a moral murder of the one you judge, because you distort his image before people. Therefore, beloved, instead of spending hours gossiping about others, hold yourself accountable instead for a few minutes daily for what you did throughout the day, and in this way you escape the judgment of God. And if you see your brother fallen, say to yourself: perhaps he will repent of it, while I may fall into it tomorrow.

2.3.0.en: Because of the abundance of God's kindness and longsuffering toward your sins, do you despise His mercies, that is, does fear of Him disappear from your heart?!

2.4.0.en: Does your heart grow harder, and do you persist in sin day after day, thus adding to the account of your sins new sins every day?

2.4.1.en: Therefore take heed, beloved, for God will reveal His wrath against those who did not make use of the period of His mercy and the time of His forgiveness throughout their life on earth. When their life ends, they will then receive a just punishment from God (Rev 20:11-15).

2.4.2.en: Perhaps you now also understand, beloved, why God is patient with the wicked who trouble you, and does not punish them now so that their harm to you might cease. The reason is that God's longsuffering includes all mankind, including you also, so that He may give everyone an equal opportunity to repent.

2.5.0.en: This verse is plain and strongly declares that purely intellectual, theoretical faith alone is not enough to obtain salvation, but there must be good works, which will be the measure of recompense, since God asks of us a faith translated into good works (the doctrine of faith and works). This is a reply to some heresies that proclaim the sufficiency of faith alone for salvation. (Mt 16:27, 2 Cor 5:10, Jas 2:17-24, Rev 2:23.)

2.6.0.en: Here St. Paul affirms the importance of works once more, explaining the reward of those who persevere in good work with all patience, without slackness or weariness, desiring not the glory, honor, and positions of the passing, false world, but true glory in eternal life, when God wipes every tear from their eyes, crowns them with a crown of glory and honor, and satisfies them with what eye has not seen and ear has not heard.

2.7.0.en: St. Paul brings us back once more to the contentious, who are from the fanatical Jewish party, who do not follow the truth but incline in their hearts and conduct toward sin; these will reap the indignation and wrath of God upon themselves. He explains that the cause of evil is distance from God (they do not obey the truth), just as the source of goodness is faith and obedience to God.

2.8.0.en: Here he puts the wicked among the Jews before the wicked among the Gentiles in receiving punishment, because the Jews received more privileges than the Gentiles in spiritual knowledge.

2.9.0.en: St. Paul puts the righteous among the Jews before the righteous repentant among the Gentiles in glory and honor, because they knew God before them, and so they labored and grew spiritually more than the Gentiles who returned to God.

2.10.0.en: God shows no partiality to anyone. Whoever received more spiritual knowledge from God is punished more if he is wicked, and rewarded more if he is righteous, for his striving after knowledge and carrying out the truth.

2.10.1.en: Imitate God in not showing partiality. If someone appeals to you in some problem, judge according to the truth, and do not favor your relatives or friends. How many marriages have been destroyed because each party and his family did not judge justly and did not admit their faults, casting all the blame and condemnation on the other party.

2.11.0.en: After St. Paul spoke of the justice of God, he answered for us a question that puzzled people for a long time: how will God judge the Gentiles although they did not receive the Law, that is, the law of Moses, as the Jews did? And what is the fault of children born to Gentile fathers and raised far from the knowledge of the law of Moses? The answer is that God has provided the Gentiles with a natural law, which is the conscience. Every person is born by nature equipped with this moral law, and the written law of Moses is in reality nothing but a bringing out of the law of conscience written on the tablets of the heart. Therefore, while the erring Jew is judged according to the law of Moses, the Gentiles who are without the law, that is, without the law of Moses, are judged according to the law of conscience. And the phrase "shall also perish without law" means that the Mosaic law will not be a witness against him.

2.12.0.en: It is obvious that those who know and understand the commandments of the Law are not the righteous, as the Jews thought, but those who carry out the commandments of the Law, whether the law of Moses or the law of conscience.

2.13.0.en: The Gentiles who do not have the law of Moses, when they do by nature the commandments that are in the law of Moses, that is, spontaneously from within their own consciences, and become obedient to God, their conscience becomes their law, because conscience is a voice from God in man.

2.14.0.en: In this St. Paul has praised some of the Gentiles who, by their good works, showed and proved that God's natural law is written on their hearts more deeply than it was written on the two tablets of stone for the Jews.

2.14.1.en: Their conscience also bearing witness: Just as the law of Moses will be the witness against the Jew on the Day of Judgment, so the conscience of the Gentile will be a witness to the thoughts of his heart, which are divided into two parties:

2.14.2.en: A party that accuses (accuse), that is, reproves the person for wrong deeds.

2.14.3.en: A party that excuses (excuse), that is, finds an excuse for the person for his wrong deeds.

2.14.4.en: Perhaps this is the eternal struggle in man between good and evil. And the conscience here is the witness over man as to who prevailed: the accusing thoughts of good, or the excusing thoughts of evil?

2.15.0.en: This judgment will take place on the Day of Judgment when God judges the secrets, that is, the secrets of hearts and hidden sins, but by a greater standard, which is according to the commandments of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

2.15.1.en: If you have enjoyed the knowledge of Christ and His commandments, be careful to live in Him lest you be judged on the last day, especially when you find that some non-Christians have applied these commandments under the guidance of their conscience.

2.16.0.en: St. Paul mocks the duplicity of Christians of Jewish origin, for they teach one thing and do another. They did not rely on the blood of Christ the Redeemer but on being Jews of the chosen people, whom God set apart as a people dedicated to Himself, and distinguished among all the peoples of the earth by giving them the Law written by the finger of God on the tablets of the Law.

2.17.0.en: He also rebukes their reliance on their knowledge of God, and their discerning of the things that differ, that is, the difficult issues of religion, such as love of God and fear of Him, mercy and leniency, firmness and severity... and so on.

2.18.0.en: By abundance of knowledge you became a guide of the blind, that is, the ignorant in spiritual knowledge, and a light to those in darkness, that is, the Gentiles living in the darkness of sin.

2.19.0.en: The Apostle Paul continues his rebuke of the Jews for their outward show, since the Jew considers himself:

2.19.1.en: An instructor of the foolish: that is, a teacher of those who are ignorant of the knowledge of God, guiding them to the truth. A teacher of babes: since classes were held in the synagogue to teach the young.

2.19.2.en: The form of knowledge and of the truth: The Jew is concerned that his outward appearance should show that he is great in knowledge and truth.

2.20.0.en: What hypocrisy and deceit by which you deceive yourself and others! You command people to abstain from sins like theft and adultery, and you abhor, that is, you call for hatred of, idols, yet you permit yourself theft and adultery and the robbing of the costly idols found in the temple of the pagans.

2.21.0.en: You boast that you know and respect the Law, but by transgressing the commandments of the Law and not carrying them out, you dishonor God Himself, because you give no weight to His word.

2.22.0.en: The final result of this is that unbelievers blaspheme, that is, they deny the religion that God established, and even reject God Himself because of your conduct.

2.22.1.en: Examine yourself, my brother, lest you be a stumbling block to others, and what you teach others, make sure that you try to apply it first in your own life, so that your teaching will be deeper and more powerful and more convincing to those who hear you.

2.23.0.en: Circumcision profits the Jew if he does the commandments of the Law, but if he is a transgressor, that is, one who does not carry out the commandments, he has become like a Gentile who does not know God, that is, uncircumcised (not circumcised).

2.24.0.en: If the uncircumcised Gentile keeps the Law, he is truly counted as one of the circumcised children of God.

2.25.0.en: The uncircumcised, who keeps the commandments of the Law out of his conscience, will be a judge of the circumcised Jew, who knows God's commandments and does not carry them out.

2.26.0.en: Then who is the true Jew? Of course, he is the one whom God praises.

2.26.1.en: For the word Jew in Hebrew means (praise), and for what does God praise him? Of course not for the circumcision of the flesh.

2.27.0.en: The one whom God praises is the one whose heart is circumcised, that is, from whom sin and iniquity have been removed by the knife of the Holy Spirit, and not only whose body is circumcised according to the commandment of Scripture. This is the true Jew, who seeks the praise of God and not the praise of people.

2.27.1.en: In short, beloved, do not rely on some outward appearances in formal worship so that people may praise you, but let your outward worship be joined to worship of the heart and purity of heart. And do not boast that you are an Egyptian from among the sons of the martyrs, and that your country was visited by the Holy Family, and that it has many monasteries and shrines, but see whether your works glorify God and gladden His heart and the hearts of those martyrs?!

2.27.2.en: Justification by faith and not by the works of the Law
